beats.trigger: From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, it's a title, but this is the topic I came for

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: the thing I've been trying to do all year is framed as impossible, so I want to see the argument

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: nothing new. I have an example already: our internal AI search that nobody opens

beats.trigger: Select** the smallest shareable form (share context / share a skill / share the output / share an interface) for the outcome the teammate wants moved
beats.got: nothing new. A list of verbs, though 'smallest shareable form' is a useful phrase

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I don't hesitate, I just build. The question is a bit uncomfortable, because nobody has asked me for any of it

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: JTBD framing, I know it from product work. Fine, but familiar

beats.trigger: If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.
beats.got: a specificity test for the agent's output. It's quick and I can apply it, and the agent read my files so the interview was actually about my setup

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: that is exactly how I pick things. My reason for the sales setup was the platform, not the outcome

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a handoff between exercises

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new, just setup for the next two steps

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: one load-bearing obstacle instead of a list of ten. For me it came out as nobody owning it after I get bored, which is a bit rude to read

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: my technical plan was done in ten minutes and the people plan was all UNASSIGNED. That is my weekend sales project in one picture

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new, it's a handoff

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: nothing new. Plans are hypotheses, sure

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: the sales team's spreadsheet is the competitor and I never considered it. That is a useful way to put it

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: three failure stories written in advance. I haven't done that for agents before, only for code, and the strongest story was social, not technical

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: the summary of the day. 'Shopping' is a fair name for what I do

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a transition into the lecture

beats.trigger: The interview earned its keep when it found a third outcome past speed and quality: a dependency removed, an anxiety gone, a scope widened.
beats.got: nothing new, since I just did this in the exercise. The third-outcome check is a small useful tip

beats.trigger: The work lives in the memory you curated, in the corrections you made every time a summary rounded a corner, in the judgement you brought to output that looked fine and was not.
beats.got: my agents work because I correct them constantly. I skip the review step and still get good output only because I have the judgement in my head. A teammate won't have that

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: context, boundary and checks copy easily. Accountability does not, and that is why 'shared agent' products feel hollow

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: our rollout dashboard counts seats, and seats are access, not use

beats.trigger: we know more than we can tell.
beats.got: nothing new that I can use. It's a philosophy quote, a bit soft for me

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: the interface is where it stops being solo work. A fair sentence but nothing to act on

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: a real failure story. Good build, fifteen people, fun workshop, and then no decision, because leadership never owned the analysis. I know that pattern from my own exec team

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: the switch conditions come out small and concrete. For sales it means a sales lead using it first, not me

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: nothing new. Adoption is their call, not mine

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding
beats.got: empty owner fields are the real status of the project, not a to-do. I still need to check who maintains my sales thing

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: nothing new. A standard review loop. The 'edit just the section' tip is useful though

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
beats.got: nothing new. Save the chat, and the one-line next step goes in a file

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a recap of what I already took in

beats.trigger: Come to Module 8 without one tested assumption or named person and you'll be reconstructing the contact while the opening exercise is already using the evidence.
beats.got: I actually have to talk to a person before module 8 or I'll fall behind. That is a concrete cost, so I probably will

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a teaser for the next module

take_homes: you can't share the agent. you share context, a skill, an output or an interface, and the thing that doesn't copy is someone answering for it
before building anything for another team, ask which job they have and what they use now. the spreadsheet is the competitor, not nothing
an empty owner in the people plan is the actual status. my weekend sales build had no maintainer

monday.move: drop the org-wide sales build. ask one person in sales how they prep for a customer call today, and what would have to be true for them to stop using their spreadsheet. write down the answer and don't build anything
monday.who: head of sales ops (haven't picked a name yet, someone in sales who'd tell me it's pointless)
monday.stop_condition: if they say there's no job here, or can't name a person who'd own it after me, I shelve it
monday.blocker: my urge to just build the thing first, and then who would maintain it

misconception.why: the line about judgement applied to output that 'looked fine and was not' describes my own habit of skipping review. it works for me only because I carry the judgement in my head, and a teammate wouldn't. I still think checking is mostly for beginners when I'm the one doing it, so this is shaken, not changed

one_line: first half is stuff i already know, but the 'you can't share an agent, only context, skill, output, interface' part and the empty people-plan columns hit my sales project right where it hurts. worth it for anyone who builds faster than their org asks for it.
